quotes: There are two approaches to providing a vapor retarder (barrier) for an insulation system for refrigerant piping:
A low-permeance sheet, film, or mastic-type vapor retarder with a permeance of ≤0.02 perm on the outer surface of the insulation system
An insulation material with a permeability/thickness combination that yields a permeance of ≤0.02 perm, sealed at all of the circumferential and longitudinal joints with vapor retarder sealant

requirements.topic: Refrigeration: maximum system permeance and the below-0°F tightening
quotes: Insulation materials should be protected by a continuous vapor retarder system with a maximum permeance of 0.02 perm, either integral to the insulation or as a separate vapor retarder material applied to the exterior surface of the insulation. At operating temperatures below 0°F, strongly consider requiring the vapor retarder to have a maximum permeance of 0.01 perm.

Service life of the insulation and pipe depends primarily on the installed water vapor permeance of the system, comprised of the permeance of the insulation, vapor retarders on the insulation, and the sealing of all joints, seams, and penetrations.
It is recommended that overlap and tape joints prepared using the Standard C1809 procedure also be required to have a permeance of ≤0.02 perm, the same as the vapor retarder material.
With refrigeration equipment operating at 35°F or lower, the problem may be severe.

For these reasons, insulation materials with high resistance to moisture (low absorption, low permeability, and low wicking) should be used for refrigerant piping operating at temperatures below 35°F.

requirements.topic: Mechanical systems (Fundamentals ch. 23): pipe, tank and equipment
quotes: Pipe, Tank, and Equipment Applications. Insulation materials used on mechanical systems operating at below-ambient temperatures must be covered by a continuous vapor retarder system that utilizes components whose water vapor permeance does not exceed 0.02 perm, with the exception of mastics (see below). Alternatively, a low-permeability insulation material of sufficient thickness to achieve this permeance level (i.e., that acts as its own vapor retarder) can be used without a separate vapor retarder, assuming all joints are properly sealed. At operating temperatures below 0°F, strong consideration should be given to employing vapor retarder system components with a maximum permeance of 0.01 perm, or those of zero permeance. Products used in these applications include ASJ, monolayer films, laminate jackets, pressure-sensitive tape, mastics and sealants and low or zero-permeability insulation.

There are two approaches to providing a vapor retarder (barrier) for an insulation system for below-ambient piping. The first is the use of a low-permeance sheet, film, or mastic-type vapor retarder with a permeance of ≤0.02 perms on the outer surface of the insulation system. The second approach uses an insulation material with a permeability/thickness combination that yields a permeance of ≤0.02 perms, which is sealed at all of the circumferential and longitudinal joints with vapor-retarder sealant.

In addition to requirements that the permeance of the vapor retarder material be no greater than 0.02 perms, it is recommended that overlap and tape joints, prepared using the C1809 procedure, also not exceed this threshold.

requirements.topic: Fundamentals ch. 23: vapor-pressure difference drives the choice (conditioned vs unconditioned space)
quotes: Typically, in buildings located in humid climates, vapor pressure differentials in unconditioned spaces are significantly greater than in conditioned spaces. For example, in a conditioned space at 75°F and 50% rh, the vapor pressure differential across the insulation system, on 42°F chilled-water lines, is less than 0.20 in. Hg. For below-ambient insulated pipes running in humid unconditioned spaces, the vapor pressure differential across the insulation system can be as great as 0.80 in. Hg in areas of the continental United States, and even greater in places with tropical climates. Hence, for insulated below-ambient pipes running in humid unconditioned spaces, the vapor retarder may need to be of lower vapor permeance than for those same pipes running in conditioned spaces.

Outdoor pipe insulation may be vapor-sealed in the same manner as indoor piping, by using an insulation material with a permeability/thickness combination that yields a permeance of ≤0.02 perms that is sealed at all circumferential and longitudinal joints with vapor retarder sealant, or applying added weather protection jacketing without damage to the vapor retarder and sealing it to keep out water.

requirements.topic: Fundamentals ch. 23: mastics are the stated exception; achieved permeance depends on thickness
quotes: It can be difficult to achieve permeance as low as the sheet vapor retarder in use under typical application conditions and using typical methods. Water-borne products are not as vapor-resistant as the solvent-borne ones that are finding less and less acceptance due to VOC limitations. Here it is critical to adhere to manufacturer application instructions to achieve proper thickness of application and acceptable vapor resistance.
Material permeability is a function of the thickness applied, so this must be very carefully controlled and monitored during installation.

requirements.topic: MIDG mastic service classes and permeance targets
quotes: Permeance of vapor retarder mastics will vary greatly ranging from 0.5 perms to <0.01 perms depending on the mastic type and performance requirements.

Cryogenic insulation systems require specialized engineering beyond the scope of this document. Mastics and coatings for these uses have very low permeability (<0.02 perms) and include specialized vapor stop coatings with extremely low service temperature limits (down to -320°F) and solvent based thermoplastic rubber (Hypalon) mastics.
Low temperature service mastics should have permeance of <0.02 perms.
Cool or cold service insulation includes insulation of chilled water piping, air conditioning ductwork and other systems operating between 33°F and ambient.
The vapor retarder system, including any sheet facing materials and mastics, should have permeance <0.05 perms per ASTM C 755.
In this case a water based mastics with permeance <0.5 perms are typically acceptable for vapor sealing punctures (from hangars or pins) and seams in the facing on interior applications.
If the insulation is not faced with a vapor retarder jacket or at insulation terminations or over bare insulation the mastic should have a permeance less than 0.05 perms.
These mastics have higher permeance, > 1.0 perm, than vapor retarders and will allow water vapor to pass through them while repelling liquid water.

requirements.topic: MIDG moisture-blocking design principle (qualitative, no number)
quotes: The design must incorporate the following: 1) a vapor retarder with suitably low permeance; 2) a joint-and-seam sealing system that maintains vapor retarding system integrity; and 3) accommodation for future damage repair, joint and seam resealing, and reclosing after maintenance.
Higher vapor pressure differences typically require a vapor retarder that that has a lower permeance to control the overall moisture pickup of the insulated system.
Some low-permeability insulation materials are considered to be vapor retarders without any additional jacket material.
3.4.4 Vapor Retarder shall have a maximum permeance of 0.02 perms for applications at or below 32°F and a maximum permeance of 0.030 perm for applications above 32°F.

3.4.3 When operating temperature is ≤32°F or when a permeance of 0.02 perms or better is required, butt joints shall be wrapped with either two layers of 3” wide Saranex 520 CX Vapor Retarder Tape or a single layer of 3” wide Saranex 560 CX Tape. When operating temperature is >32°F, butt joints shall be wrapped with a single layer of 3” wide Saranex 520 CX Tape.
Refer to ASTM standards C755, C921, and C1136 for information on selection and specification of vapor retarders.

requirements.topic: ASTM C755 (public scope only; its numeric transmission values are paywalled)
quotes: 1.1 This guide outlines factors to be considered, describes design principles and procedures for water vapor retarder selection, and suggests water vapor transmission values appropriate for established criteria. It is intended for the guidance of design engineers in preparing vapor retarder application specifications for control of water vapor flow through thermal insulation. It covers commercial and residential building construction and industrial applications in the service temperature range from −40 to +150°F (−40 to +66°C).

Application specifications for insulation systems that operate below ambient dew-point temperatures necessarily include an adequate vapor retarder system. A vapor retarder system is separate and distinct from the insulation, or is provided by the insulation itself when it is has adequate vapor resistant properties and all joints are sealed against water vapor intrusion, in which case a separate vapor retarder system is not necessary.

4.3.2 It is impractical to specify an “as installed” permeance value because, due to the nature of field application, attainment of system permeance equivalent to the vapor retarder materials themselves is assumed not possible.

quotes: Low-permeability insulations are in effect “self-vapor-retarding.” There are two types of closed-cell foam insulation that have suitably low permeability for use in below-ambient applications without the use of a separate vapor retarder. Cellular glass is characterized as having zero vapor permeability and being water-proof. As such, with all joints properly sealed to achieve like vapor resistance, the insulation can be installed in virtually all applications without a separate vapor retarder. A covering or jacket of some sort to provide physical protection, is however, required.
There are flexible closed-cell foams that likewise can be used without a vapor retarder when properly sealed at seams and joints. These are typically limited to use in chilled water applications.

Flexible closed-cell materials are applied using specially formulated contact adhesives or self-sealing lap (SSL) and may require a vapor retarder closure system for high-humidity applications. Cellular glass and elastomeric foam insulation materials installed in below-ambient applications with no external VR jacket must be sealed at all circumferential and longitudinal joints with vapor retarder sealant.

classification_systems.system: ASTM C1136 flexible low-permeance vapor retarders
quotes: 1.1 This specification covers vapor retarders for thermal insulation, specifically, flexible materials with permeance of 0.15 perm (8.63 ng·Pa^–1 · s^–1 · m^–2) or lower and surface burning characteristics of 25 flame spread/50 smoke or lower. These materials are intended for use at surface temperatures of −20 to 150°F (−29 to 66°C). It does not cover mastics or barrier coatings applied in liquid form, nor materials intended for use as weather barriers.
Vapor retarders are classified based on vapor retardance and strength properties: Types I, II, III, IV, V, and VI.
All-Service Jacket (ASJ) is used for pipe, tank, and equipment applications and meets ASTM C1136, types I-IV, or X.
Monolayer plastic films that meet ASTM Specification C1136 Types VII or VIII are used primarily on pipes, tanks and equipment.
Zero Permeance Laminations generally consist of two layers of polyester film and a center layer of nominal 1 mil aluminum foil and are designed to conform to ASTM C1136, Type IX.

The 6 mil PVDC film meets the permeance requirements of Class A, "Extremely low permeance" or 0.01 perms maximum. classification_systems.system: ICC building-envelope vapor retarder classes (context only; for wall/roof assemblies, not pipe insulation)
quotes: The 2018 supplement to the International Codes (ICC 2018) lists three water vapor retarder classes, determined according to ASTM E96 dry-cup method.
Class I: 0.1 perm or less
Class II: more than 0.1 perm but less than or equal to 1.0 perm
Class III: more than 1.0 perm but less than or equal to 10 perm
classification_systems.note: K-FLEX (R18) calls Insul-Tube 'a Class 1 vapor retarder per ASHRAE' without saying which scale; the only vapor-retarder class scale read in an ASHRAE source is this envelope scale (Class I ≤0.1 perm, R6), which is much looser than the 0.02 perm pipe-insulation criterion (R1, R2).

discrepancies: Above 32°F: JM (R20, J31) allows up to 0.03 perm; ASHRAE (R1, R2) applies 0.02 perm to all below-ambient service; MIDG (R9) cites <0.05 perm per ASTM C755 for the 33°F-to-ambient system. The simulator should let the user pick the governing document rather than merge these.
Below 0°F: ASHRAE (R1, R2) says strongly consider ≤0.01 perm; JM (R20, J31) keeps 0.02 perm for everything at or below 32°F (using Saranex 560 CX at and below 0°F per J31).

Elastomeric without a separate retarder: ASHRAE Refrigeration (R1) says use an exterior retarder in refrigeration piping unless ≤0.02 perm-in; Fundamentals ch. 23 (R2) says flexible closed-cell foams can be used without one when sealed, 'typically limited to use in chilled water applications'; Armacell (R16) says the built-in retarder 'eliminates need' with no temperature limit; K-FLEX (R18) says additional protection 'may be necessary' on cold surfaces under 'continuous high humidity'. AP ArmaFlex publishes 0.05/0.08 perm-in and K-FLEX Insul-Tube <0.01 perm-in (see material_permeability), so by the R1 criterion only Insul-Tube's published figure is at or below 0.02 perm-in.

R1 says elastomeric 'vapor permeability can be as low as 0.1 perm inch' (its Table 2 lists 0.1, the ASTM C534 Grade 1 maximum), while the AP ArmaFlex (0.05) and K-FLEX Insul-Tube (<0.01) data sheets publish lower values.

definitions.quote: Water vapor permeance M is the steady-state water vapor flux by diffusion through a flat layer, induced by a unit partial water vapor pressure difference across that layer, in lb/ft^2 · h · in. Hg.
Water vapor resistance Z is the reciprocal of water vapor permeance, in ft^2 · h · in. Hg/lb.

Water vapor permeability μ_p is the steady-state water vapor flux through a unit thickness of homogeneous material in a direction perpendicular to the isobaric planes, induced by a unit partial water vapor pressure difference, under specified conditions of temperature and relative humidity. Units are lb/ft · h · in. Hg.

Permeability is usually expressed in grains/h · ft · in. Hg and permeance in grains/h · ft^2 · in. Hg. Whereas permeability refers to the water vapor flux per unit thickness, permeance is used in reference to a material of a specific thickness. For example, a homogeneous material that is 2 in. thick generally is assumed to have half the permeance of a 1 in. thick material, even though permeances of many materials often are not strictly proportional to thickness.

definitions.explanation_quote: That is: One grain of moisture passing through a 1square foot area of a material or structure in 1 hour, as induced by 1 inch of Mercury partial vapor pressure differential

Permeability is a measurement of a material property; it can be calculated only for homogenous materials such as insulation with no facing or coating. It is an inappropriate term for use with facings.

method_for_simulator.statement: Steady-state vapor flow through a flat layer: flux per unit area m_v [grains/(h·ft²)] = Δp/Z = M·Δp (R5 Eq. 37 with Z = 1/M by R5's definition). Total flow through area A: W [grains/h] = M [perm] × A [ft²] × Δp [inHg]. Mass in pounds = grains / 7000 (R14, R7). Layers in series: Z_total = Σ Z_i = Σ 1/M_i (R7), M_total = 1/Z_total. For a homogeneous layer with permeability μ [perm-in] and thickness L [in], the flat-layer permeance is μ/L (R5: 'a homogeneous material that is 2 in. thick generally is assumed to have half the permeance of a 1 in. thick material').
method_for_simulator.derivation_note: The product form W = M·A·Δp is the flux equation multiplied by area; it is not printed in that exact form in any source read. All factors and their units are sourced (R5, R7, R10, R14).
